Authorizes visa bans and asset freezes against foreign individuals and entities responsible for serious human rights abuse or significant corruption anywhere in the world. It was enacted as part of the FY2017 defense authorization.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: Pub. L. 114-328](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/114/public/328){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 22 U.S.C. 10101 et seq.](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/10101?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Sanctions on those responsible for gross violations of human rights against people exposing government wrongdoing or exercising basic freedoms.
- Sanctions on officials and associates involved in significant corruption.
- Implemented through Executive Order 13818 (2017), which uses a broader standard of 'serious human rights abuse'.
- Congressional committees and nongovernmental groups may recommend targets.

## Why it matters

It generalized the Russia-specific Sergei Magnitsky Act of 2012 and has been copied by the European Union, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia. In practice it runs on [IEEPA](ieepa-1977.qmd) authority and it travelled to enactment inside [the annual NDAA](ndaa-annual.qmd).

## Current status

In force. Its original six-year sunset was removed in 2022 by Pub. L. 117-110.

[Last checked November 10, 2026.]{.checked}
